33.1: A story told as a conversation! Two rivers, the Vipāś (Beas) and the Śutudrī (Sutlej), rush down from the mountains like two racing horses, or like two mother cows licking their calf.
33.2: Sent by Indra, the rivers flow toward the sea as if riding chariots. They swell with waves and run to meet each other.
33.3: The rishi Viśvāmitra speaks: 'I have reached the most motherly river, the wide, blessed Vipāś.' The two rivers flow together like two mothers caring for one calf.
33.4: The rivers answer: 'We are flowing with our waves to the home the gods made for us. Once we start, nobody can stop us. Why is the poet calling us?'
33.5: Viśvāmitra (the son of Kuśika) asks politely: 'Please wait a little at my friendly words. Holy rivers, rest a moment on your journey.'
33.6: The rivers reply: 'Indra dug our channels when he killed Vṛtra, who had blocked us. The god Savitṛ with his lovely hands leads us, and we flow wide at his command.'
33.7: The rivers continue: 'Indra's brave deed must always be praised — he cut the serpent Ahi to pieces and broke the blockers, so the waters could flow.'
33.8: The rivers tell the poet: 'Never forget this conversation, singer — people in the future will repeat it.' (And here we are, still reading it today!) 'Be kind to us in your songs.'
33.9: Viśvāmitra asks: 'Sisters, listen to the poet who has come from far away with carts and wagons. Bow down low and let us cross easily — keep your water below our wheels.'
33.10: The rivers agree: 'We will listen to you, singer. Like a mother bending down to feed her baby, we will bend low for you.' Kind words worked!
33.11: Viśvāmitra says: 'As soon as the Bharatas, our people, have crossed, then flow swiftly again.' He asks only for what is needed and then lets the rivers be free.
33.12: The Bharatas crossed safely — the poet won the rivers' kindness. 'Now swell with your waves, bring riches, fill your channels and flow on quickly!'
33.13: A last wish: may the waves not break the cart's pins and straps, and may the two oxen who pulled the cart stay safe and healthy. The poet cares even for the animals.

62.1: This hymn praises many gods, three verses each. It starts with Indra and Varuṇa: 'Long ago you helped those who loved you without even being asked. Where is that glory now?' The poet gently reminds the gods of their kindness.
62.2: The worshipper keeps calling Indra and Varuṇa for help. He asks them, together with the Maruts, Heaven and Earth, to hear his call.
62.3: The poet asks Indra and Varuṇa for wealth and strong families, and for protection from the goddesses of shelter, and from Bhāratī and Hotrā, goddesses of worship.
62.4: Now three verses to Bṛhaspati, the lord of prayer and wisdom: 'Be pleased with our offerings and give good things to the one who brings you gifts.'
62.5: 'Worship the pure Bṛhaspati with your songs at every ceremony. I pray for a strength that nobody can break.'
62.6: Bṛhaspati is called the best: strong like a bull, never fooled by anyone, able to take any form he wishes.
62.7: Next, Pūṣan, the shining god who protects travellers and paths: 'Here is our newest song of praise, sung for you.'
62.8: 'Accept my song kindly and bless my sincere thoughts, the way a groom welcomes his bride with love.'
62.9: Pūṣan sees all living things at a single glance. The poet asks him to be our helper — like a good guide on a journey.
62.10: This is the famous GĀYATRĪ MANTRA! 'We think about the wonderful light of the god Savitṛ; may he inspire and guide our thoughts.' It does not ask for things — it asks for a bright, good mind. Millions of people chant it every day.
62.11: Still to Savitṛ: with understanding and sincere hearts, we ask the god for our share of good fortune.
62.12: Wise singers worship Savitṛ with hymns and rituals, moved by their own inspired thoughts. Savitṛ is the power that wakes up our minds.
62.13: Now three verses to Soma, the sacred plant juice. Soma goes to the meeting place of the gods to sit in the seat of Ṛta, the true order.
62.14: 'May Soma give healthy food to us and to our animals — to two-footed and four-footed creatures alike.' The prayer includes the animals too.
62.15: 'May Soma make our life strong, defeat what harms us and sit in our gathering.'
62.16: Last, Mitra and Varuṇa, the wise pair: 'Sprinkle our pastures with ghee and the sky with sweetness' — a poetic way to ask for good rain and rich grass.
62.17: 'You rule far and wide, happy when people praise you, with great might and pure laws that last forever.'
62.18: The poet Jamadagni ends: 'Praised by Jamadagni's song, sit in the place of truth, drink Soma, you who make truth stronger.'
